headings.title: The Standard Anatomical Position
headings.content: The **standard anatomical position** serves as the universal reference point for all human body descriptions in healthcare. In this posture, the person stands upright with the feet flat on the floor and slightly apart. The upper limbs hang at the sides, while the palms face forward with thumbs pointing away from the body. The head and eyes look straight ahead. Healthcare professionals use this standardized stance to avoid confusion when describing injuries, surgical sites, or pain locations, regardless of how the patient is actually positioned during an examination.

headings.title: Anatomical Planes of the Body
headings.content:
Body planes are imaginary flat surfaces that pass through the body to divide it into specific sections. These planes help clinicians visualize internal structures during imaging procedures like CT scans and MRIs.

- **Sagittal plane**: A vertical line that divides the body into right and left portions. When it runs directly down the exact middle, it is called the midsagittal or median plane.
- **Frontal (coronal) plane**: A vertical line that splits the body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) sections.
- **Transverse (horizontal) plane**: A horizontal line that cuts across the body, creating superior (upper) and inferior (lower) parts, often referred to as a cross-section.

headings.title: Directional Terms
headings.content:
Directional terms describe the location of one body structure relative to another. Learning these pairs makes clinical handovers precise.

| Term | Opposite | Definition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Superior** | Inferior | Toward the head or upper part of a structure |
| **Inferior** | Superior | Away from the head or toward the lower part |
| **Anterior (Ventral)** | Posterior | Toward or at the front of the body |
| **Posterior (Dorsal)** | Anterior | Toward or at the back of the body |
| **Medial** | Lateral | Toward or at the midline of the body |
| **Lateral** | Medial | Away from the midline of the body |
| **Proximal** | Distal | Closer to the origin of a body part or attachment |
| **Distal** | Proximal | Farther from the origin of a body part or attachment |

headings.title: Body Cavities
headings.content: The body contains internal spaces called cavities that protect, separate, and support internal organs. The two main divisions are the dorsal and ventral cavities. The dorsal cavity houses the brain and spinal cord within the cranial and spinal cavities. The larger ventral cavity contains visceral organs and splits into the thoracic cavity and the abdominopelvic cavity, separated by the muscular diaphragm. The thoracic cavity encloses the heart and lungs, while the abdominopelvic cavity holds digestive, urinary, and reproductive organs.

headings.title: Abdominopelvic Regions and Quadrants
headings.content: To accurately document pain, tenderness, or masses in the abdomen, nurses use two mapping methods. The four-quadrant method divides the area using a vertical and a horizontal plane intersecting at the umbilicus, creating the **Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ)**, **Left Upper Quadrant (LUQ)**, **Right Lower Quadrant (RLQ)**, and **Left Lower Quadrant (LLQ)**. For more detailed mapping, the nine-region method uses two vertical and two horizontal lines, creating regions such as the umbilical, hypogastric, and right iliac regions.
